citation: ghostty src/config/Config.zig, macOS keybind defaults - the five 'natural text editing' binds. The arrow routing is measured, see docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 5.
why: Input precedence is fixed (architecture.md): the keymap gets first refusal on every chord, and only what it declines is reported toward the pane. The chords here are the ones people press without thinking in a terminal that is not a text field, and getting one wrong is not a crash - it is a key that quietly does something close to right, which is the kind of bug that survives for months. These are Muster's own policy, so the citation is the whole oracle: there is nothing external to record against.

cases.name: cmd+backspace is unix-line-discard
cases.why: The chord that prompted the whole table. Without it ⌘⌫ deletes a single character and a person holds the key down instead, which looks broken. Readline's 0x15 does the same job, and being a control code it means the same thing whatever the pane has negotiated.

cases.name: cmd+left is start of line
cases.why: macOS line motion, mapped to readline's ctrl+A. Same reasoning as ⌘⌫: the platform's chord, the terminal's control code.

cases.name: cmd+right is end of line
cases.why: The pair of cmd+left, mapped to readline's ctrl+E.

cases.name: alt+left is word motion
cases.why: Word motion is an escape prefix rather than a control code, because that is what readline binds it to. ESC b.

cases.name: alt+right is word motion forward
cases.why: The pair of alt+left. ESC f.

cases.name: a bare arrow is the pane's
cases.why: The daemon encodes every key against the pane's own modes, so a bare arrow needs nothing from the keymap: application cursor mode decides between SS3 and CSI, and the daemon can see which is on. It is left to the pane like any other key.

cases.name: shift+arrow is the pane's
cases.why: The same as a bare arrow, and the pair with cmd+left and alt+left above: those are bound, so the modifier is what selects between the keymap and the pane.

cases.name: an unmodified ordinary key is the pane's
cases.why: The keymap takes only what it has a reason to take. Anything else belongs to the program in the pane, and a keymap that swallowed plain keys would be a terminal that cannot type.

cases.name: an unmodified backspace is the pane's
cases.why: Only the cmd-modified form is bound. Plain backspace has to reach the program, which is what deletes the character.

cases.name: cmd+a is not bound here
cases.why: Guards the shape of the table rather than a chord anyone presses: `super` is bound with backspace and the arrows, and a lookup that keyed on the modifier alone would swallow every cmd chord on the keyboard.

cases.name: which side of the keyboard a modifier came from does not change the chord
cases.why: The encoder needs to know left command from right; a binding does not. A keymap that matched on the side bits would work on one half of the keyboard and not the other, which is the kind of bug a right-handed developer never sees.

cases.name: a key release never fires a binding
cases.why: Under a kitty profile that reports releases, firing on both edges sends everything twice - the same shape as the doubling bug that made typing `hello` produce `hheelllloo`.
